> I am currently using the default for window sizes, and have modified includedaycrit to a lower value to hopefully salvage more data. But currently, I am only getting 15 participants' data out of a possible 95 in the part 2 analysis. Is there anything I can do to change here, so that I could possibly get more data out?

Please inspect the GGIR output to understand why days and individuals are excluded. Never guess parameter setting but consider your study protocol and participant instructions, run GGIR and inspect its output, read up on parameter documentation, and use all that knowledge combined to tailor your GGIR analyses.

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
> is it correct to assume that these nights are included in part5 because they are being estimated based on other available data even though the night data has been removed from part4?

Yes, that is correct.

If you feel that estimates are concerningly wrong, consider parameter data_cleaning_file which allows you to specific which window should be excluded from part 5.

Another option is to work with the full daysummary csv report from part 5 as stored in the results/QC folder. Here, remove the nights you do not want to work with and then aggregate this to person level outside GGIR.

Best wishes,

Vincent

Hi,
I am a little confused of results of the same individual in two different version of GGIR. We aimed to calculate the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) using the "sleepreg" function, which is compatible only with GGIR version 2.0.0, not the latest version. To proceed, I had to remove the latest GGIR version from my laptop and reinstall version 2.0.0. However, I'm encountering issues with the results in this version: individuals from time zones other than EST (such as PST and Mountain Standard) show significantly different outcomes in the older GGIR version compared to the latest. It appears that the results from GGIR 2.0.0 may not be accurate, though I'm uncertain about the cause of this discrepancy between the two versions.
I've attached my R code, as well as a presentation comparing actigraphy double plots, sleep onset, wake times, and sleep duration across both versions to highlight these differences. Additionally, I've noticed that some summary report files generated are 0-byte files with no data output.
One more question: the "sleepreg" function uses files from the ms3.out folder within GGIR, but it sometimes encounters 0 or negative values, preventing SRI calculation.
This results in the following error: "simpleError in onoffvector_cons_miscl[NAon] <- NA: only 0's may be mixed with negative subscripts." Could you advise on resolving this error?

Dear Arpita,

GGIR release 2.0-0 was from May 2020, Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) was added to GGIR in release 2.4-3 in 2021 as you can see in the GGIR change log <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/news/news.html>.

There is no 'sleepreg' function in GGIR, and I suppose you are using https://github.com/dpwindred/sleepreg and that this is actually an error in their software? Note that it has been a very peculiar effort by them to develop complementary functionality to GGIR without communicating about it with me as GGIR maintainer. By the time they had published their work I had implemented SRI inside GGIR rendering their secret effort a complete waste of time. If you have issues with their code please contact them. However, I would recommend using the sleep regularity index as implemented in GGIR, which is also much better able to handle missing data.

Release 2.0-0 is known to have major bugs as I have communicated with collaborates and with co-authors (Lane, Weedon etc) of the Windred paper in 2021. The fact that they kept on using 2.0-0 has been their decision. For me reflections on why GGIR has changed between version, see also my response in this <https://groups.google.com/g/rpackageggir/c/nvI-gZQ2LzI/m/0nYBSEVVAQAJ> thread.

If you have specific suggestions about inaccuracies or bugs in the latest GGIR version then I look forward to your report.

Thanks,

Vincent

Hi Yue,

Sorry for the delay. I was able to replicate your problem and noticed that the QC plot from part 2 explains what is happening:

For most nights GGIR detects the night of nonwear as expected, but on day 5 the participant also does not seem to have worn the accelerometer twice during daytime. Next, GGIR then labels the time in between as nonwear, because of the build in assumption that wear surrounded by a lot of nonwear cannot be informative. See also the documentation <https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/chapter3_QualityAssessment.html#non-wear-detection> on this.

I think the best solution is to ignore this day via the day/night inclusion criteria.

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] ENMO_fullRecordingMean not generated
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cecilie,

I suspect this is because you have strategy = 2 and recording of 48 hours not starting at midnight. As a result you only consider the middle 24 hours as valid, which may not be enough to trigger any meaningful weighted average calculation as there is only 24 hours. You could as well use the normal day level estimate of ENMO.

Note that we renamed strategy to data_masking_strategy for readability, but it still works.

To verify this try data_masking_strategy = 1, which will tell GGIR to consider all data in the recording. This should trigger the calculation of ENMO_fullRecordingMean because there is more than 24 hours of data. I cannot find back in the code right now whether we have a specific threshold on this or whether this just emerged from the fact that the code needs more than 24 hours of data to do any meaningful weighting. ... it is code I wrote in 2012 and I seem to not have changed it in all those year, which is either reassuring or concerning depending on how you look at it.

Best,
Vincent

> Hi Javad,
>
> Good question. I am currently involved in a study that looks into this and we hope to submit our work to a journal this summer... so my hands are bit tight to answer this in detail. However, I can say the following:
>
> GGIR has been designed to be minimally sensitive to sample frequency. For example, GGIR does not attempt to rely on specific very short lasting events or high frequency signal components. Also, GGIR intentionally does not attempt to detect patterns in the raw data.
>
> The real problem, I think, is that a few accelerometer brands are poor at capturing the acceleration of movement consistently across sample frequency settings. Therefore, I think your question should be accelerometer brand specific.
>
> You give the impression that resampling is a solution to a lack of comparability of raw data, but resampling itself can also introduce discrepancies and on top of that resampling does not address a systematic bias caused by sampling rate. For example, if X Hertz results in 10% lower magnitude of acceleration then resampling will not be able to fix that. A better solution would be to either identify the source of the bias and address it, or to identify problematic accelerometer brand and sample rate combinations and discourage their use.
>

> > Good question. I am currently involved in a study that looks into this and we hope to submit our work to a journal this summer... so my hands are bit tight to answer this in detail. However, I can say the following:
> >
> > GGIR has been designed to be minimally sensitive to sample frequency. For example, GGIR does not attempt to rely on specific very short lasting events or high frequency signal components. Also, GGIR intentionally does not attempt to detect patterns in the raw data.
> >
> > The real problem, I think, is that a few accelerometer brands are poor at capturing the acceleration of movement consistently across sample frequency settings. Therefore, I think your question should be accelerometer brand specific.
> >
> > You give the impression that resampling is a solution to a lack of comparability of raw data, but resampling itself can also introduce discrepancies and on top of that resampling does not address a systematic bias caused by sampling rate. For example, if X Hertz results in 10% lower magnitude of acceleration then resampling will not be able to fix that. A better solution would be to either identify the source of the bias and address it, or to identify problematic accelerometer brand and sample rate combinations and discourage their use.

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Manual cleaning of GGIR part 4 output
messages.body_plain:
Hello Pilar,

Did you consider using the sleep estimates stored in part 5 output? They reflect sleep estimates guided by sleeplog, if sleeplog present for a certain night, or sleep estimates guided by the build-in algorithm if sleeplog is not present for that night.  An additional advantage of the part 5 output is that this directly excludes invalid days, in contrast to the part4 _full report, which does not offer any data cleaning. In part 5 you may want to focus on timewindow = "WW" or "OO" as those reflect the full SPT window, in contrast to "MM" which accumulates sleep per calendar day.

What you could indeed do is:
Process the data for the first time as you have done.
Correct or impute the sleep log based on your observations.
Consider the data_cleaning_file parameter to skip specific nights or days in part 4 and 5.
Reprocess part 4 and 5 with the new sleep log and optionally data_cleaning_file parameter.

Does this address your needs?

If not, it would be helpful to aim for a situation where GGIR can help you do most of the work to avoid that you and other GGIR users end up doing a lot of custom data handling outside GGIR which introduces more work for everyone and higher risk for errors and inconsistencies between studies. So even if you use a different strategy it would be good to hear about it.

Best wishes,

Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] M10_mean_peakLUX and M10_max_peakLUX
messages.body_plain:
Dear Arpita,

By default LUX is first summarised in GGIR part 1 as peak LUX per 15 minute epoch. The variables you refer to represent the mean and max value in these peak LUX values across M10, respectively.

> If so, would you say these are variables associated with the circadian rhythm of the wearer, where individuals with earlier chronotype may have lower mean peak LUX (if they wake up before it is sunny)?

In comparison with the mean or max lux per full day or during waking hours only, these variables attempt to standardise the role of sleep duration and time in bed duration. For example, if a person is awake for 20 hours a day they have a much higher change of accumulating a lot of light during those hours compared with a person awake for 14 hours. It then becomes unclear whether it is sleep duration or actual day time behaviour that drives differences in light exposure. So, these variables should aid you in better understanding what drives differences in light exposure. Dr. Séverine Sabia proposed these variables and asked me to implement them. You may find more motivation in our publication: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36494722/

Best wishes,

Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: Code for non-wear detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Khadija,

I see I never replied to your message...

The narrative documentation on nonwear can be found here:
https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/chapter3_QualityAssessment.html#non-wear-detection

The first stage of nonwear detection happens in GGIR part 1, which essentially entails labelling each 60 minute window with a nonwear score to reflect the number of axes that meet the nonwear criteria. The essential code can be found here: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/R/detect_nonwear_clipping.R

The second stage of the nonwear detection is to filter short lasting wear surrounded by a lot of wear and to collapse the nonwearscore into a simple binary classification, which happens in GGIR part 2 and more specifically in
https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/R/g.weardec.R
which is called from https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/R/g.impute.R.

... I know function names and structure could be improved but due to lack of resources priority has been elsewhere.

Best wishes,

Vincent

Thanks for the quick reply!

To set the record straight: so far we have not used idloc --> so idloc = 1 (default), which means that GGIR takes the ID from the .bin file. Here I assume that the ID is extracted from line 39 “Subject Code:”. However, there are spaces in this line as already described.
The file name is of course without spaces.

Unfortunately, I cannot provide any of our patient data records for data protection reasons. However, I have created a short recording.
The file name (automatically defined by the GENEActiv software) is “12345_left wrist_071023_2024-11-28 12-33-45.bin”.
Line 39 in the file is “Subject Code:12345               ”.

The extraction of the ID from the file name before “_” ( idlock = 2) works well for us - I tried this yesterday in the data set with approx. 50 21-day recordings.

However, if I want to use idloc = 1 for our data sets (and I assume that this is the case for all GENEActiv data sets) and want to avoid the IDs being cutt off in visualization_sleep.pdf, then you would either have to open each .bin file and remove all spaces after the ID in “Subject Code” (line 39), or you would have to teach ID loc to ignore spaces after the ID.

This is our used code:

library(GGIR)

GGIR(                   # Erklärungen siehe https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/GGIRParameters.html

  #  To Do! ####
  maxdur = 21,
  datadir = "C:/GENEActiv/data/Test/"
  outputdir = "C:/GENEActiv/results",

  mode = c(1,2,3,4,5),          # gibt an, welcher der GGIR Parts (1 bis 6) ausgeführt werden soll
  overwrite = TRUE,             # Ob vorherige Ausgaben im Outputordner überschreiben (TRUE)
  do.report = c(2,4,5),         # Reportdateien, die erstellt werden sollen (möglich von Part 2, 4 und 5)
  idloc =2,                     # definiert Quelle der ID (1 --> aus .BIN-Datei - Problem mit Leerzeichen bei visual_sleep.pdf, 2 --> alles vor "_" --> https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/GGIRParameters.html#idloc)

  # 3.3. GGIR Part 2 ####
  # === Basisanalyse (non-wear detection, basic descriptive summary of accelerations)
strategy = 1,
hrs.del.start = 0,
hrs.del.end = 0,
includedaycrit = 16,
includenightcrit = 16,
qwindow = c(0,24),
mvpathreshold = c(100),       # MVPA = Moderate or Vigorous activity; Beschleunigungsschwelle für die MVPA-Schätzung [in mg?]; bei Angabe mehrerer Werte (,), werden mehrere MVPA Werte errechnet
bout.metric = 4,
excludefirstlast = FALSE,

  # 3.4. GGIR Part 3 + 4 ####
  # === für Schlafanalyse
def.noc.sleep = 1,
outliers.only = FALSE,
criterror = 4,
do.visual = TRUE,

  # 3.5. GGIR Part 5 ####
  # === für Analyse der physical activity und Reporterstellung
threshold.lig = c(30),        # Nummerischer Schwellenwert für leichte körperliche Aktivität (in Abgrenzung zu Inaktivität). Bei Angabe mehrerer Werte =c(30,40), dann erfolgt die Analyse für die einzelnen Schwellwerte separat; Bezieht sich auf ENMO [mg]

threshold.vig = c(400),       # Siehe „threshold.lig“; grenzt moderate vom schwerer Aktivität ab
boutcriter = 0.8,             # Bezüglich „mvpathreshold“ (in Part2): Anteil des Zeitabschnitts, welcher über der bei „mvpathreshold“ angegebenen Schwelle liegen muss
boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in> = 0.9,          # Gibt den Anteil des Zeitabschnitts an, welcher unter der Schwelle „threshold.lig“ liegen muss, damit das zur Inaktivität gezählt werden kann
boutcriter.lig = 0.8,         # Siehe „boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in>“; Anteil des Bout (Zeitabschnitts) zwischen den Grenzen t…lig und t…mod
boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8,        # Siehe „boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in>“ Boutanteil, der oberhalb des Grenzwerts threshold.mod liegen muss
boutdur.in <http://boutdur.in> = c(10,20,30),     # ???? https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/GGIRParameters.html#boutdur-in
boutdur.lig = c(1,5,10),      #
boutdur.mvpa = c(1,5,10),     #

messages.subject: Missing MVPA data only
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am looking at physical activity data. I am using Axivity AX6 accelerometers and two RStudio scripts to process the data. I have used the scripts to good effect, having processed around 700 pieces of individual data. I run two scripts, the first processes the data using a study specific version of the GGIR script for PA. The second extracts specific data relevant to the study, including calibration error, measurement duration, wear duration (minimum 3day validation criteria), intensity gradient, mean acceleration, sleep duration, inactive minutes, light intensity activity, vigorous intensity activity and moderate to vigorous intensity activity. These data are sourced from part 2 / 4 / 5 GGIR script output files.

I ran both scripts today and found something I have not encountered before. One participant met the validation wear time criteria, had data for intensity gradient, mean acceleration, inactive activity and light intensity activity,  however there were no data for sleep duration, vigorous intensity activity nor MVPA (i.e.., the columns were blank). MVPA is our primary outcome for the trial and so important. I looked into this and the participant did not wear the accelerometer at night, so I can understand why the sleep column was blank, however they had wore the accelerometer during the day on 4 days meeting the validation criteria, resulting in some PA data being included in the output. I then looked at the raw part2 summary files where the relevant data were sourced from and this participants data were blank in both the vigorous and MVPA columns.

Does anyone know why these columns would be blank? Is there a work around? I imagine not, but I would be keen to understand why we are missing primary outcome data for this participant, especially when the output did include intensity gradient, mean acceleration (both also taken from part2 summary file), inactive minutes and light intensity minutes.

To be specific, we used the following items for the output:
Vigorous intensity: part2_summary / Column RE / AD_MVPA_E5S_B1M80._T400_ENMO_0.24hr
MVPA:  part2_summary / Column QS / AD_MVPA_E5S_B1M80._T100_ENMO_0.24hr
I look forward to hearing others thoughts on this.

Many thanks,

Gareth
